ligg-talocruralia-lateralia.summary: Three separate ligaments running from the lateral malleolus to the talus and calcaneus. Because they are much weaker than the deltoid ligament on the medial side, they are the structures most often injured in ankle sprains.
facts: Anterior border of the lateral malleolus – neck of the talus; flat and the weakest ligament; tight in plantar flexion
Tip of the lateral malleolus – lateral surface of the calcaneus; cord-like; passes deep to the fibular tendons; supports both the ankle and the subtalar joint
Malleolar fossa of the lateral malleolus – posterior process of the talus; the strongest lateral ligament and the most rarely torn
First the anterior talofibular, then the calcaneofibular, last the posterior talofibular ligament tears
clinical: The anterior drawer test assesses the anterior talofibular ligament, the talar tilt (inversion stress) test the calcaneofibular ligament.
Repeated sprains can lead to chronic lateral instability; surgical repair (Broström) may be performed.
tus: 85% of ankle sprains are inversion injuries and the anterior talofibular ligament tears first.
The calcaneofibular ligament is the only lateral ligament that contributes to both the ankle and the subtalar joint.

lig-deltoideum.tr: Deltoid ligament (medial ligament of the ankle)
lig-deltoideum.summary: A very strong, triangular ligament fanning out from the medial malleolus to the navicular, calcaneus and talus. It prevents the ankle from opening with eversion and external rotation.
facts: Tibionavicular part (to the navicular tuberosity and spring ligament), tibiocalcaneal part (to the sustentaculum tali)
Anterior and posterior tibiotalar parts (to the medial surface of the talus); the deep part is the main stabiliser preventing lateral shift of the talus
Limits eversion, supports the medial side of the ankle and the medial arch
So strong that in forced eversion the medial malleolus may break off (avulsion) before the ligament tears
clinical: If the deltoid ligament tears in an eversion-external rotation injury, the talus shifts laterally in the mortise; untreated, ankle arthrosis develops.
In adult acquired flatfoot, failure of tibialis posterior is accompanied by laxity of the deltoid and spring ligaments.
tus: The deep tibiotalar part of the deltoid ligament is the most important structure preventing lateral shift of the talus.
In eversion injuries the medial malleolus may fracture instead of the deltoid ligament tearing (Pott fracture mechanism).

art-subtalaris.summary: The joint between the inferior surface of the talus and the upper surface of the calcaneus. Most of the movements raising the inner and outer borders of the foot (inversion and eversion) take place here; it allows walking on uneven ground.
facts: Anatomical subtalar joint: posterior calcaneal facet of the talus – posterior talar facet of the calcaneus. The clinical (functional) subtalar joint also includes the talocalcaneonavicular joint with the anterior and middle facets
Synovial plane joint (functionally a uniaxial joint with an oblique axis)
Interosseous talocalcaneal ligament (in the sinus tarsi, the strongest), lateral, medial, anterior and posterior talocalcaneal ligaments; the calcaneofibular ligament also supports it
Inversion-eversion (components of supination-pronation)
A tunnel between talus and calcaneus opening laterally; contains the interosseous ligament and fat
clinical: Calcaneal fractures usually involve the subtalar articular surface and can lead to permanent subtalar arthrosis.
Sinus tarsi syndrome causes persistent pain on the lateral side of the foot after ankle sprains.
tus: Inversion and eversion occur mainly at the subtalar and transverse tarsal joints, not at the ankle joint.
Talocalcaneal coalition is the commonest coalition of the talocalcaneonavicular joint and shows the 'C sign'.

art-tarsi-transversa.summary: S-shaped joint line formed by the talonavicular and calcaneocuboid joints, between the hindfoot and the midfoot. Together with the subtalar joint it takes part in inversion-eversion.
facts: Talocalcaneonavicular joint (head of talus – navicular and spring ligament) and calcaneocuboid joint

Bifurcate ligament (Y ligament: calcaneonavicular and calcaneocuboid parts), talonavicular ligament, plantar calcaneonavicular ligament (spring ligament), plantar calcaneocuboid ligament (short plantar ligament), long plantar ligament
Inversion-eversion, abduction-adduction of the forefoot
One of the amputation levels of the foot (Chopart amputation)
clinical: Chopart injuries can be missed as ankle sprains; a sprain of the bifurcate ligament causes pain on the lateral side of the foot, in front of the sinus tarsi.
After Chopart amputation the stump may drop into equinus (plantar flexion) through the unbalanced pull of the Achilles tendon.
tus: The plantar calcaneonavicular (spring) ligament supports the head of the talus from below and is the key ligament of the medial arch.
The two limbs of the bifurcate ligament run from the calcaneus to the navicular and the cuboid.

artt-tarsometatarsales.summary: The joints between the three cuneiforms and the cuboid and the bases of the five metatarsals. The locking of the 2nd metatarsal base between the cuneiforms and the Lisfranc ligament give this joint its stability.
facts: Synovial plane joints; three separate synovial cavities (medial, middle, lateral columns)
Medial cuneiform – 1st metatarsal; intermediate and lateral cuneiforms – 2nd and 3rd metatarsals; cuboid – 4th and 5th metatarsals
Strong interosseous ligament from the medial cuneiform to the base of the 2nd metatarsal; there is no ligament between the bases of the 1st and 2nd metatarsals
Dorsal and plantar tarsometatarsal ligaments (the plantar ones are stronger), cuneometatarsal interosseous ligaments
clinical: A Lisfranc injury (tarsometatarsal fracture-dislocation) occurs with a fall onto a plantar-flexed foot or crushing of the foot from behind; plantar bruising is typical and about 20% are missed at first presentation.
The Lisfranc line is one of the levels used for foot amputations.
tus: Bruising of the sole (plantar ecchymosis) should suggest a Lisfranc injury.
On X-ray the medial border of the 2nd metatarsal should line up with the medial border of the intermediate cuneiform; a shift indicates a Lisfranc injury.

arcus-pedis.summary: The bones of the foot do not form a flat platform but two longitudinal arches and one transverse arch. The arches distribute load between the heel and the metatarsal heads and act as shock absorber and lever in walking; they are maintained by the shape of the bones, by ligaments and by muscles.
facts: Calcaneus, talus, navicular, three cuneiforms and 1st–3rd metatarsals; high and flexible; its keystone is the head of the talus
Calcaneus, cuboid, 4th–5th metatarsals; low, close to the ground; its keystone is the cuboid
Cuneiforms, cuboid and metatarsal bases; most marked in the forefoot
Plantar aponeurosis (the most important – 'windlass' mechanism), long plantar ligament, plantar calcaneocuboid ligament, plantar calcaneonavicular (spring) ligament
Tibialis posterior, fibularis longus, tibialis anterior, flexor hallucis longus, intrinsic muscles of the sole
sections: In the push-off phase of walking, when the big toe dorsiflexes, the plantar aponeurosis winds around the metatarsal heads and tightens; it pulls the heel forwards, raises the medial arch and turns the foot into a rigid lever.
clinical: Flatfoot (pes planus) is collapse of the medial arch; in adults the commonest cause is failure of the tibialis posterior tendon.
Pes cavus (high arch) may be seen in neuromuscular diseases such as Charcot–Marie–Tooth.
Plantar fasciitis is degeneration of the plantar aponeurosis at its attachment to the calcaneus; heel pain with the first steps in the morning is typical.
tus: The keystone of the medial longitudinal arch is the head of the talus, that of the lateral arch the cuboid; the spring ligament (plantar calcaneonavicular) supports the head of the talus from below.
The tendons of fibularis longus and tibialis anterior form a 'stirrup' under the foot that supports the transverse and medial arches.
